analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $6.65 by 2000 and automatically adjusts it for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 1998 with 9 Senate cosponsors but never left committee and never got a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage in three steps, starting at $5.65 an hour in September 1998 and reaching $6.65 by 2000. After 2001, the wage would rise automatically each year with the cost of living, so it would stop losing value to inflation. The bill was sent to the Senate Labor Committee the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum wage, who would see a raise of $1.50 an hour over three years, and workers whose pay is tied to the minimum wage. Because the wage would be indexed to the Consumer Price Index, their pay would keep up with rising prices instead of eroding between congressional votes.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets the federal minimum wage at $5.65 an hour beginning September 1, 1998, $6.15 beginning September 1, 1999, and $6.65 beginning September 1, 2000.

Beginning September 1, 2001, the minimum wage would be adjusted each year by the Secretary of Labor to reflect increases in the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, so the wage floor rises automatically with the cost of living.

Indexing to inflation removes the need for Congress to pass a new law every few years just to keep the wage from losing value, which is how the minimum wage historically fell behind prices between legislative fights.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum-wage labor, especially labor-intensive service businesses such as restaurants and retail, would bear higher wage costs. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through prices, and opponents typically argue that higher wage floors reduce entry-level hiring.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises labor costs for employers of minimum-wage workers, and the Congressional portion of the record shows no study of those effects; standard economic concerns are that businesses could respond with fewer entry-level jobs, reduced hours, or higher prices.
The bill contains no small-business phase-in, tax offset, or regional adjustment: the $6.65 floor applies nationwide on the same schedule regardless of local wage levels.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers at or near the minimum wage, a $1.50-an-hour increase plus automatic inflation adjustment is a substantial, permanent gain, and automatic indexing is the stronger design because it stops the wage floor from silently eroding. The cost falls on employers of low-wage labor and potentially on prices, with the familiar trade-off that some entry-level employment could be affected; the bill's flat nationwide schedule offers no transition help for small or seasonal employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on January 27, 1998 and referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 1998 in the Senate on January 27, 1998, joined by 9 Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
No committee vote, floor action, or roll call ever followed; the last recorded action in the bill's history is the referral to committee.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and a bill that is never reported out of committee dies at the end of a Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers, who avoided the $1.50-an-hour wage increase and automatic inflation adjustments the bill would have imposed, while minimum-wage workers went without a raise.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on January 27, 1998.

for.name: 8 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Wellstone, Moseley-Braun, Mikulski, Kerry, Torricelli, and Boxer, who joined in its introduction.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Called for a federal minimum wage increase in early 1998, aligning with the bill introduced the day of his State of the Union address.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Jim Jeffords (R-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 27, 1998 and took no further action; no markup or committee vote is recorded.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott (R-MS) and the majority controlling the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; because it never left committee, it never came up for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 cosponsors were Senate Democrats, and the bill sat in committee under a Republican majority without ever reaching the floor; no roll-call vote was ever taken.

industries.note: Restaurants are the largest employers of minimum-wage workers, so a $1.50-an-hour federal increase with automatic inflation adjustments would directly raise their labor costs. Blocking the bill preserved the existing wage floor for these employers.

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: Businesses that rely heavily on minimum-wage labor would bear the higher wage costs on a fixed national schedule. The industry's interest in stopping the bill ran against the wage gains the bill offered workers.

Millions of workers at or near the federal floor would have gained $1.50 an hour by 2000, plus automatic cost-of-living increases thereafter. The bill's failure left them at the then-current minimum wage with no indexing.
